title: Theo and the Giant Cookie
markdown:
Sunlight burst through leaves. Golden stripes painted Theo’s workshop. “Today,” Theo boomed, “is picnic day!” He grabbed his toolbox, not for building, but for measuring. Poppy the dormouse was beside him. Her nose twitched. Her whiskers vibrated. Pure excitement. “Squeak! Picnic!” she chirped, bouncing onto Theo’s shoulder. The air smelled like damp earth and sweet berries.

They dashed past busy ants marching in single file. Tiny feet pattered. Birds sang a spectacular show of chirps and trills. A perfect morning symphony. They met Ms. Vale by the whispering stream. Her basket bobbed like a happy boat. Ms. Vale was a whirlwind of bright colours and tinkling laughter. “Oh, my dears!” she chirped, her bird-like eyes sparkling. “I brought the most spectacular treat for our picnic!”

She pulled out a cookie. A giant golden cookie. Bigger than Theo’s sturdy boot, sparkling with sugar crystals, the sort of cookie that looked as if it had eaten other cookies for breakfast.

Poppy gasped. Her little chest puffed out like a tiny balloon. Theo blinked. His cheerful hum stopped. “That’s… one big cookie, Ms. Vale,” he said, voice full of wonder.

“Indeed! And there’s enough for all of us, surely!”

But Theo looked at the single massive cookie on a bright red checkered cloth. He saw three friends. He saw one giant cookie. How could they share it fairly? It looked so delicious.

Theo tapped his chin. His brow furrowed. He tried to break it. No. The cookie was too tough. It resisted his mighty tugs. Poppy, eager for a taste, took a tiny nibble. All she got was a crumb. They needed a clever plan, not brute force, not tiny nibbles.

Suddenly, with a wobble and a roll, a big chunk broke off. Poppy squeaked. “Oops!”

Theo, ever practical, picked up the biggest piece. “Don’t worry, Poppy!” He opened his toolbox. He found his trusty ruler. “This big bit is one part,” he said. He measured the rest. “And this is another part, exactly the same size!” He carefully sliced the rest into two perfect equal halves with his sharpest knife.

Poppy’s little eyes widened. “Ooh! Two halves!”

Theo grinned. “Exactly. We’re splitting it into equal parts. Two nice equal halves for now.”

He tapped his chin again. “But we’re three.” He looked at Poppy. He looked at Ms. Vale. “Two halves are good, but not quite enough for three hungry friends. What if we take these two halves, and cut each half into two more equal bits?” He carefully measured and cut. Now there were four pieces, all looking perfectly the same.

“Four pieces!” chirped Poppy. “Four equal pieces!”

“These are called quarters. Four equal quarters. But we still need three equal pieces, one for each of us.”

Ms. Vale’s eyes sparkled. “What if we try to make three equal pieces from the very start?”

Theo’s hammer tapped. Tap-tap-tap. He took out his special measuring tape, with its tiny perfect markings. “Okay.” He carefully marked the giant cookie in three distinct spots. With his sharpest knife, he made three perfect clean cuts. Each piece was exactly the same size. They were thirds.

Theo placed three perfect thirds of the cookie on a large green leaf. Poppy eagerly took one. Theo took one. Ms. Vale took one. They munched happily. The sweet buttery aroma filled the air. The cookie was crumbly, delightful, and absolutely delicious.

“See?” Theo said between contented bites. “When we divide things into equal parts, like halves, or thirds, everyone gets a fair share. It’s like building a strong bridge. Every piece needs to be just right.”

Poppy nodded vigorously. “Fair share!”

Ms. Vale laughed. “And Theo, your clever measuring and careful cuts made it all possible. You built fairness, just like you build bridges.”

Theo beamed. He loved building bridges, but he also loved building fairness. What other wonderful secrets could be discovered by carefully dividing things up? He wondered what else in the world could be shared so perfectly—and he could not wait to find out, preferably before the ants marched over and asked for quarters of their own.
characters: Theo (bridge builder), Poppy (excited dormouse), Vale (tinkling picnic teacher)
